newsitem.title: UK: Betting shop firm William Hill may be put on sale.
newsitem.headline: Betting shop firm William Hill may be put on sale.

text.p: British betting chain William Hill could be sold off as debt-laden owner Brent Walker Plc seeks to cash in on its last major asset, the company said on Thursday.
Leisure group Brent Walker confirmed that it was examining the options for William Hill, Britain's second- largest bookmaker with about 1,700 shops across the country.
Brent Walker owes its bankers more than 1.3 billion pounds ($2.1 billion), while share analysts put a provisional price tag of about 500 million pounds on William Hill.

The company, built up by boxer-turned-businessman George Walker, has shrunk so much that William Hill is all that remains of what was once Britain's biggest leisure chain comprising marinas, a film arm and more than 1,000 pubs.
Boom had turned to bust by 1991 when the banks stepped in, forcing out chairman Walker and engineering a complex restructuring.
The group on Thursday announced an operating profit of 62.5 million pounds for 1996, a 22 percent increase on the previous year.

Profit before tax and interest came in at 216.5 million pounds, helped by the sale of the Pubmaster chain of inns and the settlement of a dispute with Grand Met over the purchase price paid for William Hill in 1989.

A company spokesman said there were several options under consideration for William Hill, ranging from a trade sale to a flotation. "Our raison d'etre is to maximise the return to stakeholders," he said.

A decision must be taken in the next few months as Brent Walker's lending arrangements with its banks terminate at the end of the year. These will have to be extended should the company decide to keep the business.
"I think they will be looking to realise the value of the asset to avoid refinancing," said analyst Greg Feehely of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
Looking at potential purchasers, Feehely ruled out market leader Ladbroke Group Plc as any deal would run into monopoly concerns.

Brewing and leisure group Bass Plc, which has some 930 betting shops in its Coral chain, has declined comment on market speculation linking it with William Hill. But Bass is believed to have looked closely at the business.

Feehely said that any Bass deal could also face regulatory hurdles and that the company might have to promise to sell off some shops. Stanley Leisure Plc is seen as a possible bidder for some of these excess sites.
Stanley is Britain's fourth largest bookmaking chain, with around 500 shops.

A reduction in the government betting levy and the introduction of fruit machines to betting shops have helped bookmakers to recover after they were badly hit by the launch of the national lottery in 1994.
